paragraphs.heading: Belief before the evidence
paragraphs.text: A prior, short for prior probability distribution, is the probability distribution you assume for an uncertain quantity before any evidence is taken into account. For instance, a prior could describe the relative shares of voters expected to back a particular politician in a coming election. The quantity need not be something you can observe; it may be a parameter of a model or a latent variable rather than an observable one.

paragraphs.heading: How a prior gets updated
paragraphs.text: In Bayesian statistics, Bayes' rule says how to combine the prior with new information to reach the posterior distribution, the distribution of the quantity given the new data. The words prior and posterior are relative to a particular piece of data. In the past, people often had to pick priors from a conjugate family for the likelihood, so the posterior would be easy to work with and of the same family. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods are now widely available, which has made this less of a worry.

paragraphs.heading: Where priors come from
paragraphs.text: There are many ways to build a prior. It may come from past information, such as earlier experiments, or from the purely subjective judgement of an experienced expert. When nothing is known, an uninformative prior can be used, justified by the principle of indifference. In modern work, priors are also often picked for what they do mechanically, such as regularization or feature selection.

paragraphs.heading: Informative and strong priors
paragraphs.text: An informative prior carries specific, definite information about a variable. Take the temperature at noon tomorrow: a sensible prior is a normal distribution centred on today's noon temperature, with a spread equal to how much the temperature varies from day to day. A strong prior is an informative prior whose information outweighs the information in the data. In that case, the posterior that comes out of the analysis would be little changed from the prior.

paragraphs.heading: Weakly informative priors
paragraphs.text: A weakly informative prior gives only partial information. It nudges the analysis toward answers that fit existing knowledge without tying it down too tightly, and it prevents extreme estimates. For tomorrow's noon temperature in St. Louis, one could pick a normal distribution centred on 50 degrees Fahrenheit, with a standard deviation of 40 degrees. That only loosely keeps the temperature between 10 and 90 degrees. The aim is regularization: keeping conclusions within a reasonable range.

paragraphs.heading: Uninformative priors
paragraphs.text: An uninformative prior, also called flat or diffuse, expresses only vague or general information. Such a prior can still carry objective facts, for example "the variable is positive". The simplest and oldest rule for building one is the principle of indifference, which gives every possibility the same probability. When estimating parameters, an uninformative prior usually gives results close to conventional statistics, because the data often carry more information than the prior.

paragraphs.heading: The ball under three cups
paragraphs.text: An example due to Jaynes makes the idea concrete. A ball sits under one of three cups, labelled A, B and C, and you know nothing else about where it is. A uniform prior, p(A) = p(B) = p(C) = 1/3, seems the only reasonable choice, because swapping the labels leaves the problem unchanged, and only the uniform prior keeps your predictions unchanged under such a swap. Yet this prior is not a feature of the world: the ball really is under one cup, and the probabilities make sense only for an observer who does not know which.
